facts.raw_span: a 2‐day history of right lower‐extremity numbness and pain
manual muscle testing of the right tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus was 3/5
gastrocnemius and flexor hallucis longus were 4/5
deep‐tendon reflexes were normal
Straight‐leg‐raising was positive at 70 degrees
the femoral‐nerve stretch test was negative
Plain radiographs showed degenerative scoliosis at L5–S1
Lumbar MRI demonstrated a right‐sided disc herniation at L5–S1
Initial peroneal‐nerve conduction studies revealed a motor conduction velocity of 51.5 m/s
Ankle‐brachial indices were decreased (0.78 on the right, 0.73 on the left)
lower‐extremity arteriography showed no significant vascular lesions
right foot drop (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, flexor hallucis longus, and peroneus longus 1/5; left side 4/5)

concepts.why: The patient's symptoms of right lower-extremity numbness and pain, along with the findings of decreased motor conduction velocity and foot drop, are consistent with peroneal nerve palsy.
The patient's positive straight-leg-raising test and lumbar MRI findings of a right-sided disc herniation at L5-S1 support the diagnosis of lumbar disc herniation.
The patient's symptoms of numbness and pain, along with the findings of decreased motor conduction velocity and foot drop, are consistent with peripheral neuropathy.

The patient's decreased ankle-brachial indices and symptoms of foot drop could be consistent with vasculitic neuropathy, although the lack of significant vascular lesions on arteriography makes this diagnosis less likely.
The patient's plain radiographs showed degenerative scoliosis at L5-S1, which could be contributing to her symptoms.
The finding of decreased ankle-brachial indices despite no significant vascular lesions on lower-extremity arteriography may indicate peripheral artery disease.
